motion: Is the Canaanite conquest morally defensible as an act commanded by a loving God?

bridges.description: Connect conquest judgment to the loving yet judging God revealed across both Testaments.
Use ancient war rhetoric to limit literal total-destruction readings.
Identify military centers and corrupting institutions rather than ethnicity as the target.
Defend a unique contextual judgment without making it repeatable.
Argue that residual civilian killing or forced group removal remains morally indefensible.
Concede exaggeration while denying that it removes the moral residue.
Use Jesus and moral intuition as controls on conquest readings.
Offer historically cautious, spiritualized, and moral-error alternatives.

sections.title: Scripture and interpretive method
sections.rationale: The rival Christian hermeneutics determine how conquest commands bear on divine love.

sections.title: Historicity and war rhetoric
sections.rationale: Historical caution and exaggerated war language determine the literal scope.

sections.title: Civilian harm and moral responsibility
sections.rationale: Noncombatant targeting is the central moral dispute.

sections.rationale: The parties dispute the object and moral classification of the campaign.

sections.title: Christological alternatives and exceptional judgment
sections.rationale: The final statements directly test divine love, alternative readings, and contextual exception.

moves.speaker: Paul Copan
moves.claim: A Christ-centered reading should preserve continuity between the Old and New Testament portrayals of God.
moves.warrant: Copan says Jesus and New Testament authors retain Mosaic authority while revealing God's enemy-loving character.
moves.inference: The conquest should be interpreted within one divine character rather than assigned to a false textual deity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Copan's complete opening interpretive thesis and its qualification about unresolved tensions.

moves.attributionRationale: The sustained first-person case is Copan's; a key theological term is garbled by automatic captions.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects conquest judgment with divine love.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Christians may affirm inspiration while allowing moral error in human authorial intent and using Jesus and moral intuition as interpretive guides.
moves.warrant: Rauser distinguishes God's purpose in including a text from the human author's intent and calls moral intuition fallible but God-given.
moves.inference: This permits criticism of a violent portrayal without rejecting scripture or Christianity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Rauser's complete positive hermeneutic and its Christological conclusion. The boundaries retain the complete claim, its stated reason, and the resulting inference without unrelated host material.

moves.attributionRationale: Rauser is clear, but the Christocentric phrase and biblical reference are caption-sensitive.

moves.importanceRationale: This establishes Rauser's central interpretive route.

moves.warrant: Rauser concedes merisms but uses Rahab's family, Ai, and less-mobile inhabitants to argue that noncombatants remained at risk.
moves.inference: Reduced or uncertain numbers still require a moral justification.

moves.speaker: Paul Copan
moves.claim: The principal targets were military citadels, and the primary command was to drive Canaanites out, not exterminate civilians.
moves.warrant: Copan appeals to Richard Hess's citadel case and notes that Joshua's obedience coexists with many surviving Canaanites.
moves.inference: Military targeting, expulsion, and survivors make indiscriminate civilian slaughter a poor summary of the campaign.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Copan's complete eligible citadel and drive-out answer before he broadens to New Testament judgment.

moves.inference: Copan's defense must own the residual killing of noncombatants even if their number is smaller.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Forcibly removing Canaanite identity can qualify as ethnic cleansing or genocide even when not every person is killed.
moves.warrant: Rauser applies group-destruction concepts to killing, expulsion, and coerced cultural erasure, including the residential-school analogy.
moves.inference: Changing the target from bodies to group identity does not by itself make the conquest morally defensible.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This earlier independent passage includes the hyperbole concession and full legal-moral classification.

moves.importanceRationale: This contests the identity defense at motion level.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that cultural destruction can itself be grave group harm.

moves.speaker: Paul Copan
moves.claim: The aim was dismantling a corrupting religious-political identity rather than destroying an ethnicity.
moves.warrant: Copan distinguishes Nazi ideology from German people and cites Rahab, covenant participants, and continuing Canaanite presence.
moves.inference: If people can remain while harmful institutions and identity markers end, the action need not be genocide.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This eligible span preserves Copan's correction and full ideology-versus-people case before the frozen host-led chain.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Jesus's character and moral intuition count against a divine command to kill children, while spiritualized or moral-error readings preserve Christian scripture without endorsing slaughter.
moves.warrant: Rauser contrasts Jesus embracing a child with guiding a spear, then outlines allegorical, exilic, and moral-error approaches before closing that targeting noncombatants is intrinsically wrong.
moves.inference: Christian commitment does not require accepting a temporary exception for civilian slaughter.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains two linked closing steps—Christological control and the resulting alternative readings—and is retained because the inference would be incomplete if split from its constructive options.

moves.importanceRationale: This is Rauser's complete closing route from moral test to alternatives.

moves.speaker: Paul Copan
moves.claim: The conquest was unique, unrepeatable, and divinely supervised, and generally sound intuitions may be overridden by morally sufficient contextual factors.
moves.warrant: Copan distinguishes acts God cannot command from cases like shooting down a hijacked plane to prevent greater destruction and reiterates canonical judgment.
moves.inference: Exceptional circumstances can make foreseen innocent deaths compatible with a loving God's judgment without creating a repeatable norm.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Copan's complete final statement from uniqueness through contextual override and canonical conclusion.
